title: Delhi Destroys 2,800 Kg of Adulterated Sweets and Dairy Ahead of Festive Season
excerpt: Delhi's Food Safety Department has stepped up inspections at mandis, sweet manufacturing units and markets across the capital, putting paneer, khoya and ghee under scrutiny as festive-season demand surges.
body:
• Delhi's Food Safety Department destroyed more than 2,800 kg of unsafe dairy products — including khoya, dhaap and butter — found abandoned in unhygienic conditions at markets including Khoya Mandi and Mori Gate.
  • Lab tests found serious quality failures: all 10 khoya and cream samples from Mori Gate were non-conforming, and four paneer samples at Janakpuri Mandi tested positive for detergent.
  • Health Minister Pankaj Kumar Singh ordered the city-wide drive, with surprise inspections at sweet manufacturing units in Okhla, Badli, Nihal Vihar and Narela and 37 samples sent for laboratory analysis.
  • Intensive inspections and sampling will continue through the festive season, with officials promising strict action against anyone selling adulterated food.

Delhi Steps Up Enforcement Ahead of the Festive Rush

Delhi's Food Safety Department has stepped up inspections across the capital's food markets ahead of the festive season, destroying more than 2,800 kg of unsafe dairy products and flagging adulteration in the staples used to make festive sweets. The enforcement drive, ordered by Health Minister Pankaj Kumar Singh, puts paneer, khoya and ghee under close scrutiny as demand for milk, milk products and sweets climbs across the city.

Food safety teams inspected markets including Khoya Mandi, Mori Gate, Bagh Deewar, Sanjay Market and Janakpuri Mandi, focusing on suspected adulteration, poor storage conditions and the quality of products sold to consumers. At Khoya Mandi, Mori Gate, Bagh Deewar and Sanjay Market, officials found around 2,830 kg of unclaimed khoya, dhaap and butter lying in unhygienic conditions. The products were foul-smelling and showed signs of deterioration.

Officials made public announcements asking sellers to come forward and claim the food items. No one did. The entire stock was confiscated and destroyed at the MCD dumping site at Majnu Ka Tila under the provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.

Context & Background

The crackdown follows an August 28 directive from Singh instructing the Department of Food Safety to intensify inspection, surveillance and enforcement across Delhi as the festive season neared. The order targeted sweet manufacturing units, mandis, markets and other vulnerable locations, with a stated focus on paneer, khoya and ghee alongside sweets and other high-demand items.

Surprise inspections were conducted at sweet manufacturing units in Okhla, Badli, Nihal Vihar and Narela, as well as at the Okhla Subzi Mandi and Ghanta Ghar Subzi Mandi. Roughly 131 kg of expired food articles — including khoya, besan and atta — were identified and destroyed on the spot, while 37 samples of paneer, khoya, ghee, sweets and other products were collected for laboratory testing.

"The health and safety of Delhi's citizens is our foremost priority. With festive demand increasing, we have directed the Food Safety Department to maintain heightened vigilance across the city and ensure rigorous inspections and sampling. Special attention is being given to milk and milk products, sweets and other high-demand food items," Singh said.

Impact & Analysis

Laboratory results from the September raids show why the department is worried. All 10 samples of khoya and cream collected from Mori Gate were found non-conforming when analysed at the State Laboratory. At Janakpuri Mandi, enforcement teams inspected 10 food business premises, collected 10 enforcement samples of paneer and ran spot analysis on 28 surveillance samples using the Food Safety Wheel. Four of those samples tested positive for detergent.

As a precaution, about 150 kg of paneer and 10 kg of khoya were destroyed at Janakpuri Mandi. Two enforcement samples of khoya were also collected from the Bagh Deewar–Sanjay Market area, where four samples — two paneer and two khoya — were found conforming on Food Safety Wheel testing.

"Festive preparations must not come at the cost of food safety. We will ensure that no unsafe or adulterated food reaches the people of Delhi."

— Pankaj Kumar Singh, Delhi Health Minister

Singh has directed the department to maintain heightened surveillance and continue intensive inspections throughout the festive season. The department said consumer safety remains the priority and instructed officials to take prompt and stringent action wherever adulterated or unsafe food is detected.

Diaspora Angle

For Indian families celebrating the festive season abroad, the Delhi drive carries a familiar warning: the khoya, paneer and sweets at the heart of every festival table are also the most vulnerable to adulteration when demand surges. Buyers can reduce the risk by purchasing from licensed, established sellers, checking manufacturing dates, and staying alert to off smells or unusual textures in dairy products.

What's Next

Enforcement teams will continue intensive inspections and sampling at markets, manufacturing units and food establishments across Delhi through the festive season. Laboratory findings from the 37 samples collected during the August inspections are expected to determine further action, with the government warning that anyone found manufacturing, storing or selling adulterated food will face strict penalties under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
